All at once the painter showed himself in the studio doorway and beckoned them inside with a series of quick gestures. They looked at one another and smiled.

“I am waiting for you,” he called. “Please come in. The light could not be better, and you may bring your drinks.”

They got up and strolled together along the path. A pair of green-and-white butterflies fluttered by, and a thrush started singing in the pear-tree at the garden’s corner.

“You are pleased to have met me, Mr. Gray,” Lord Henry said, regarding him.

“Yes, I am pleased now. I wonder if I shall always be?”

“Always! What a frightful word. Hearing it makes me shiver. Women love to say it. They ruin every romance by endeavouring to prolong it for ever. And the word means nothing. Between a passing fancy and a passion for life, the only distinction is that the fancy endures a little longer.”

On entering the studio, Dorian Gray rested his hand upon Lord Henry’s arm. “Then let our friendship be a passing fancy,” he said softly, colouring at his own daring. He mounted the platform and took up his pose again.

Lord Henry dropped into a spacious wicker arm-chair and looked on. Nothing disturbed the silence but the sweeping, darting brush upon the canvas, save when Hallward occasionally retreated to view his painting from farther off. Dust motes danced golden in the sloping sunlight pouring through the open door. The rich perfume of roses seemed to hang above everything.

Some fifteen minutes later Hallward laid aside his painting. He gazed at Dorian Gray for a long while, then at the portrait for as long, frowning and biting the end of a great brush. “It is completely finished,” he exclaimed at length. Bending forward, he signed the canvas in the left-hand corner with long vermilion letters.

Lord Henry approached to inspect it. Certainly it was a marvellous painting, and the likeness was marvellous too.

“My dear fellow, my warmest congratulations,” he said. “This is the finest portrait of our age. Come here, Mr. Gray, and see yourself.”

The young man started as though someone had roused him from a dream.

“Is it truly finished?” he whispered, coming down from the platform.

“Entirely,” the painter replied. “And you have been a splendid sitter today. I am immensely grateful.”

“The credit for that is wholly mine,” Lord Henry interposed. “Isn’t it, Mr. Gray?”

Dorian did not reply. He moved languidly in front of the portrait and turned to face it.

Of course he was very amusing and all that, but I was terribly disappointed. When I asked about the coat of chain mail, he just laughed and said it was much too cold to wear in England. Ah, here comes Mr. Podgers! Now, Mr. Podgers, I want you to read the Duchess of Paisley’s palm. Duchess, you must remove your glove. No, not the left one, the other.’

‘Dear Gladys, I really don’t think this is quite proper,’ said the Duchess, weakly undoing the buttons of a rather dirty soft-leather glove.

‘Nothing interesting ever is,’ Lady Windermere replied. ‘That is how the world is made. But let me introduce you. Duchess, this is Mr. Podgers, my favourite palm reader. Mr. Podgers, the Duchess of Paisley. And if you tell me that the mount of the moon on her palm is larger than mine, I shall never trust you again.’

‘Gladys, I am sure there is no such thing on my hand,’ the Duchess said seriously.

‘Your Grace is perfectly right,’ said Mr. Podgers, examining the small, plump hand and its short, square fingers. ‘The mount of the moon is undeveloped. But the life line is excellent. Please bend your wrist. Thank you. Three clear lines across it! You will live to a great age, Duchess, and be extremely happy. Ambition—quite modest; the line of intelligence—not excessive; the heart line—’

‘Now, Mr. Podgers, do tell us something indiscreet!’ cried Lady Windermere.

‘Nothing would please me more,’ he replied with a bow, ‘if the Duchess had ever been indiscreet. Unfortunately, I see very lasting affection and a strong sense of duty.’

‘Please continue, Mr. Podgers,’ said the Duchess, looking thoroughly pleased.

‘Carefulness with money is another of Your Grace’s considerable virtues,’ he continued, sending Lady Windermere into fits of laughter.

‘Economy is an excellent thing,’ the Duchess observed contentedly. ‘When I married Paisley, he owned eleven castles and not one house fit to live in.’

‘And now he has twelve houses and not one castle,’ cried Lady Windermere.

‘Well, my dear,’ said the Duchess, ‘I like—’

‘Comfort,’ Mr. Podgers supplied, ‘and modern conveniences, and hot running water in every bedroom. Your Grace is quite right. Comfort is the only thing our civilisation can offer us.’

‘You have described the Duchess’s character wonderfully, Mr. Podgers. Now you must read Lady Flora’s.’ At a nod from their smiling hostess, a tall girl with sandy Scottish hair and prominent shoulder-blades stepped awkwardly from behind the sofa. She offered a long, bony hand with fingers that broadened at the tips.

‘Ah, a pianist, I see,’ said Mr. Podgers. ‘An excellent pianist, though perhaps hardly a musician.’

Emma did not regret having lowered herself to visit the Coles. The following day brought many pleasant memories of the evening, and whatever dignity she might supposedly have sacrificed by leaving her usual select circle was surely more than repaid by the glory of her popularity. She must have delighted the Coles—good people, who deserved to be made happy! And she had left an impression that would not soon fade.

Complete happiness is rare, even in memory, and two things still troubled her. She wondered whether, by confiding her suspicions about Jane Fairfax’s feelings to Frank Churchill, she had broken the obligation one woman owed another. It was scarcely right. But the idea had been so powerful that it had escaped her, and his acceptance of everything she said was such a compliment to her insight that she found it difficult to feel certain she should have kept quiet.

Her other regret also concerned Jane Fairfax, and about this she had no doubts. She sincerely and unreservedly regretted that her own playing and singing were inferior. She bitterly lamented having been so idle as a child, and sat down to practise diligently for an hour and a half.

Harriet’s arrival then interrupted her. If Harriet’s praise had been enough to satisfy her, she would soon have felt comforted.

“Oh, if only I could play as well as you and Miss Fairfax!”

“Don’t put us together, Harriet. My playing resembles hers no more than lamplight resembles sunshine.”

“Oh, dear! I think you play better than she does. I think you are quite as good. I certainly prefer listening to you. Everyone last night said how well you played.”

“Anyone who understood music must have heard the difference. The truth, Harriet, is that I play just well enough to earn praise, but Jane Fairfax goes far beyond that.”

“Well, I shall always believe you play just as well as she does—or that, if there is any difference, nobody would ever notice it. Mr. Cole spoke about your wonderful taste. And Mr. Frank Churchill talked a great deal about your taste, and said he valued taste much more than technical skill.”

“Ah, but Jane Fairfax has both, Harriet.”

“Are you sure? I could see that she had the skill, but I didn’t know she had any taste. Nobody mentioned that. And I hate singing in Italian. You cannot understand a word. Besides, if she does play so very well, it’s only what she has to do, you know, because she will have to teach.”
